messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: adjust how distances are collected at close distances?
parts:
Kim, I think your reference to the distance sampling book is to the 1993
book. The 2001 book has more relevant comments on this topic - but in
any case, you have misunderstood what is said on p307. It says that, by
spending some time at the point, it increases the chances of detecting
all birds close to the point. It does NOT say that most detected birds
will be very close to the point - in fact, quite the reverse is
expected, as the area within say 5m of the point is very small, so tends
to hold very few birds. If you're getting lots of detections within 5m
of the point, then I suspect you have problems with assumptions. It's
possible that you're dealing with birds that for the most part aren't
detectable unless they're very close - in which case it would be better
to measure exact distances as far as possible. However, 10-min counts
are unlikely to work well if this is the case. Suppose for example that
you have a bird that isn't detectable unless it is within 5m of the
point. Suppose also that it is moving around during the 10-min count.
By waiting for 10-mins, you're increasing the chance that the bird will
move to within 5m of the point. So that is where you detect it. This
is systematically reducing detection distances, and would lead to
overestimation of density. Distance sampling is a snapshot method.
I'll send you separately a pdf of a paper of mine on this issue that
appeared in 2006 in the Auk. It explains why conventional methods can
be expected to overestimate density for species that typically move
around, and how methods can be made to work.

If you're dealing with songbirds, with surveys conducted in the breeding
season, you may want to consider surveying singing males only, as these
are much more detectable, allowing estimation with low bias and high
precision. This may force an assumption that there is on average one
female for every male, and for some species, it may be necessary to
estimate the proportion of males that can be expected to sing within a
given time interval. If you include in your survey silent females,
especially in very dense habitat, your distance distribution will be
impossible to model reliably, and estimates will be very uncertain. You
may also have the problem that even females at the point may be missed
(g(0)<1).

Personally, I think assigning birds to 10 distance intervals is no
saving over estimating actual distances. You should definitely use a
laser rangefinder - these are inexpensive these days. Even if you
detect most birds by sound alone, a laser rangefinder can be a very
useful aid for improving distance estimates - see the paper in the Auk.

Steve Buckland
